title: Wastewater disinfection under extracellular DNA exposure and antibiotic selective pressure: effects on bacterial communities and associated antimicrobial resistome
description: Antimicrobial resistance is spreading worldwide, and aquatic ecosystems play a key role within the One Health framework. In this context, wastewater treatment plants represent hotspots for antimicrobial-resistant bacteria and antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs). In this study, we experimentally investigated the effects of conventional disinfection treatments, namely chlorination and peracetic acid treatment, on the fate of a GFP-tagged plasmid carrying the aminoglycoside resistance gene aadA under antibiotic selective pressure. Quantitative Real Time PCR was used to quantify the gfp gene as a proxy for cell-associated and/or intracellular GFP-tagged plasmid DNA, as well as class 1 integron-integrase gene (intI1) as a proxy for ARG dissemination potential and anthropogenic pollution. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing was performed to characterize the bacterial community and associated ARGs. In the disinfected samples, bacterial community richness decreased together with gfp abundance, with marked reductions in Acinetobacter, a bacterial genus among the most abundant taxa detected, known for its natural competence. Although antimicrobial resistome richness decreased, the relative abundance of ARGs, particularly aadA, increased, whereas intI1 abundance did not vary significantly following disinfection. Furthermore, a metagenome-assembled genome taxonomically assigned to the family Phycocordibacteraceae was associated with a gfp-positive contig. Overall, these findings underscore the need to consider the interplay between disinfection, environmental stressors, and horizontal gene transfer, including the possible contribution of natural transformation, when assessing the potential for antimicrobial resistance dissemination in environmental systems.
